title: Nobody Sets the Price. Everybody Does.
subtitle: No committee decides what a coffee, a stock, or a house is worth. A price is a signal that emerges from millions of buyers and sellers haggling at once.
hook: Who decided a cup of coffee costs $4? Nobody. Not the café, not the government — the price emerged from a tug-of-war between what buyers will pay and what sellers will accept. A price is one of the most information-dense things in the world: a single number quietly summarizing millions of people's wants, costs, and guesses. Today: how supply, demand, and price discovery actually work.

sections.heading: The tug-of-war
sections.body: **Demand**: as price drops, more people want it. **Supply**: as price rises, sellers offer more. The price gravitates to where the two curves cross — the **equilibrium**, where the quantity people want to buy equals the quantity offered. Push the price above it and unsold goods pile up (pushing it back down); below it and shortages appear (pushing it up). Nobody steers this; it self-corrects.

sections.caption: Demand falls with price, supply rises with it. Where they cross is the price that clears the market — no one chooses it.

sections.label: Prices are messages
sections.body: A rising price screams 'we need more of this!' and pulls in producers; a falling one says 'enough, make something else.' This is **price discovery** — markets aggregating scattered information (a drought here, a fad there) into one number, faster than any central planner could. It's why shortages of a hot product don't last: the high price summons supply. Prices coordinate strangers who never speak.

sections.label: When the signal misfires
sections.body: Prices aren't magic truth. They break when there's a monopoly (one seller sets terms), hidden costs the price ignores (pollution — an 'externality'), or panic and manias (everyone buying because everyone's buying). A price reflects willingness to pay, which isn't the same as real value or fairness — a lesson markets teach the hard way in every bubble.

sections.caption: Supply, demand, and how prices are actually set.

takeaways: A **price** emerges from buyers and sellers, not a central decision-maker.
It settles at **equilibrium** — where quantity demanded meets quantity supplied.
**Price discovery** aggregates scattered information into one coordinating number.
Rising prices summon supply; falling prices redirect it — self-correcting, usually.
Prices misfire under **monopoly, externalities, and manias** — willingness to pay ≠ true value.

options: Where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
quiz.explain: It's where the demand and supply curves cross and the market clears.

quiz.q: A product suddenly gets popular and prices spike. What usually happens next?
options: The high price attracts more suppliers, easing the shortage over time
quiz.explain: High prices are a signal that summons supply — that's price discovery at work.

quiz.q: BOSS: When does the price signal FAIL to reflect real value?
options: Under monopoly, hidden externalities (like pollution), or manic bubbles
quiz.explain: Prices track willingness to pay under competition and full information. Break those conditions and the signal lies.

tg_quiz.q: Who sets the 'right' price of a coffee?
options: No one — it emerges from supply & demand
tg_quiz.correct: Right — it emerges where supply meets demand.
tg_quiz.wrong: No single person — it emerges from buyers and sellers together.
tg_quiz.explain: A price is a signal, not a decree.
